Introduction 
Welcome to TSB Bank’s 2025 Climate Statement.   
Continuing TSB’s long and proud history of doing right by our communities is 
front of mind for us, as we consider how we contribute to a sustainable future. 
Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges of our time. The impacts are 
being felt globally and locally, and New Zealand is no exception. Here we face significant 
climate-related issues including rising sea levels, increased frequency and intensity of 
extreme weather events, and threats to our unique ecosystems. These changes pose risks 
not only to our environment but also to our economy, infrastructure, and the health and 
wellbeing of our communities. 
The insights we’ve gained from our climate-related disclosure work, as outlined in this Climate 
Statement, helps us understand what climate change means for our business model. This work has 
enabled us to create our first Sustainability Strategy and Climate Transition Plan to guide how we will 
build resilience and respond to the climate-related risks and opportunities which face our bank and the 
wider financial industry, our customers and our communities. 
We know there is much more to do to achieve our sustainability and climate change goals. We are 
committed to better understanding and owning our environmental impact and being transparent and 
accountable as we progress our journey.  
Thank you for taking the time to read our Climate Statement, we look forward to updating you in future 
reports.

About this report
Important information 
This Climate Statement (Statement) is a mandatory disclosure under Part 7A of the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 
(FMCA), prepared in accordance with the External Reporting Board’s Climate Standards (NZ CS), for the year ended 31 
March 2025. It has been prepared for our primary users, being Toi Foundation Holdings Limited as our sole shareholder, 
and existing and potential customers, lenders and other creditors.
The Statement contains climate-related and other forward-looking statements and metrics, including climate related 
scenarios, transition planning, assumptions, climate projections, forecasts, statements of TSB Bank’s future intentions, 
estimates and judgements which are not and should not be considered guarantees, predictions or forecasts of TSB 
Bank’s present and future strategies, future climate-related outcomes or financial performance. These statements are 
subject to known and unknown risks, inherent uncertainties, limitations around inputs and available data, and other 
factors, many of which are beyond the Bank’s control. Readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on such 
statements in light of the significant uncertainty in climate metrics and modelling that limit the extent they are useful 
for decision-making, and the many underlying risks and assumptions may cause actual outcomes to differ materially. 
The risks and opportunities described here and in our transition plan objectives may not eventuate or may be more 
or less significant than anticipated. There are many factors that could cause TSB Bank’s actual results, performance or 
achievement of our objectives to differ materially from that described, including economic and technological viability, as 
well as climatic, government, consumer, and market factors outside of TSB’s control.
This report reflects TSB Bank’s current understanding of current and future climate related impacts, events, risks, 
opportunities and strategies as at 28 July 2025. TSB Bank has sought to provide a reasonable basis for forward-looking 
statements.  We are committed to progressing our response to climate-related risks and opportunities over time, and 
to report our progress each year, but we caution reliance on aspects of this report which is necessarily subject to the 
caveats above. While we have prepared the information in this report based on our current knowledge, understanding 
and in good faith, we reserve the right to change our view in the future. 
Reporting entity: The Statement covers TSB Bank Limited only. TSB Bank Limited has no subsidiaries. It has one 
shareholder, Toi Foundation Holdings Limited, a 100% subsidiary of Toi Foundation. References to ‘TSB’, 'TSB Bank',  
‘the Bank’, ‘we’, ‘us’ and ‘our’ mean TSB Bank Limited. For detailed information on our financial performance, please  
refer to the TSB Bank Annual Report and Disclosure Statement, available at tsb.co.nz/about/financial-information.

About TSB Bank
Who we are
TSB Bank is proudly community owned - for 175 years we have put people first, consistently 
winning customer service and product awards, and retaining our profits here for Aotearoa.  
While our roots are proudly in Taranaki, we support Kiwi and businesses right across the motu, with 
banking products, digital services and our famous personalised care. 
The Bank is owned by Toi Foundation - this is a unique part of who we are because our dividends support 
their philanthropic work. 
From our Board to our frontline, this is why our people choose to work for TSB Bank, and it means our customers 
and community are genuinely central to everything we do.
Where we’re going
By 2030 TSB Bank aspires to be the digital bank of choice, with exceptional customer experience that serves the needs of 
Aotearoa consumers and businesses, providing a genuine alternative to the major banks for passionate Kiwi.
At the centre of our TSB 2030 Strategy are our commitments to our key stakeholders – our people, customers, community, 
shareholder and regulators. 
Our rautaki sees us continuing to modernise TSB into a highly engaging digital bank, offering simple and useful products for our 
customers, so we’re the easiest bank to deal with. 
We’re achieving this through focusing on three areas: Simplify, Diversify, and Differentiate, underpinned by investing in Our People and 
Our Organisation.

Our business model
TSB operates right across the motu, with assets of $9.6 billion as at 31 March 2025, we offer banking products, digital 
services, and our award-winning customer service to predominantly personal and small to medium sized business 
customers, with residential lending making up the majority of our book.
TSB is funded primarily through the funds our shareholder, Toi Foundation, has invested and retained in TSB and retail 
deposits, with wholesale funding making up less than 1% of total funding and more than 99% of our $8.7bn deposits at 
31 March 2025 being from retail sources. Due to Agriculture’s low and declining share of our total lending portfolio we 
have included but not focused on it in this analysis. However, as set out in the Metrics and Targets section, emissions 
associated with TSB’s Agricultural lending were estimated to be approximately 39% of our financed emissions in FY25,

Current climate-related impacts
Physical risks arise as climate change leads to increasing risks of extreme weather events and gradually more progressive 
impacts such as sea level rise and ocean acidification. These risks are typically divided into:
•	 Acute – the risk of impacts from extreme weather events 
•	 Chronic – the risk of gradual impacts
Transition risks arise as an economy takes steps to mitigate physical risks and progress towards lower emissions. For 
example, low emissions policies can lead to increased costs for businesses and households, and societal preferences 
shifting towards more sustainable businesses, which risks creating stranded assets and unprofitable businesses.
Potential impacts associated with physical and transition risks can also lead to climate-related opportunities for TSB. (See 
Appendix 1 for further background information).
TSB has no current material climate-related physical or transition impacts for the year to 31 March 2025. Consequently, 
there were no material financial impacts for this period.
Physical impacts (FY25)
TSB does not consider that it has experienced material physical impacts to our credit portfolio and our operations as a 
result of climate-related events. Credit portfolio mitigating factors have been our insurance and equity requirements for 
borrowers, customers’ existing equity, and local and national government policy. 
Credit level - Some of our customers have been impacted by events that are partially attributable to climate change 
(for example, property damage from flooding) but the mitigating factors noted above were sufficient to prevent TSB 
experiencing a material credit impact in FY25.
Organisational level - We provided support to our customers who were impacted by the events noted above, but the 
operational costs associated with our response were not material to our FY25 result. There were no other material 
operational impacts from those events either as TSB buildings (where owned by TSB) are fully insured, and business 
interruption processes provide for primary customer services online and by phone. Some of our branch locations have 
been impacted (for example, branch access difficulties due to localised flooding) but the mitigating factors noted here 
prevented the operational impact being material in FY25. There were no significant IT service interruptions or supply chain 
impacts due to the above events, including from damage to data centres. 
Transition impacts (FY25)
TSB has not yet experienced any material adverse or positive credit or operational impacts from the transition to a low 
emissions economy. 
Impacts from opportunities (FY25)
We have reviewed areas for potential resource efficiency savings, emissions reductions and climate resilience, as well  
as new products to assist customers’ reduction of environmental impact (see Climate-related risks and opportunities on 
page 15).
Some Scope 1 and 2 emissions reduction opportunities were previously identified and are being actioned, however, these 
are not material to TSB’s total GHG emissions footprint including operational and financed emissions. We have reviewed 
our assessment of new product opportunities during FY25 but have not launched any associated products or services.

Scenario analysis:  
TSB climate scenarios 
The goal of TSB’s scenario analysis is to be aware of and prepared for what realistically may occur in the world as a result of climate change – to promote resilience 
under plausible future climate states. 
The scope of TSB’s scenario analysis is set by the focal question: ‘How could climate change plausibly affect our business model and strategy through the creation of 
risks and opportunities?’ 
To answer this TSB has chosen to utilise the banking sector scenario analysis provided by New Zealand Banking Association Te Rangapū Pēke (NZBA)  and focus on 
the parts of that analysis that are applicable to TSB’s business model and strategy. The sector analysis is based on three climate reference scenarios published by the 
Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), tailored to New Zealand circumstances. Further description of the scenarios and the assumptions which underlie 
them is set out in Appendix 2 - TSB Scenario Narratives.
Orderly Transition
A future world where collective action is taken towards a low carbon global economy (1.5°C scenario)
Too Little Too Late
Fragmented and delayed transition to a low carbon economy between New Zealand (early mover) and the rest of the world (fossil-
fuelled development to mid-century) (2.7°C scenario)
Hothouse
Minimal action towards a low carbon global transition, increasing levels of social, economic, and environmental degradation (>3°C 
scenario) 
Details of the time horizons used are set out in the table on the next page. 
When considering the narratives for each scenario, TSB has conducted an 
analysis of our business model, considered our value chain and focused 
on our material customer sectors of residential and commercial property 
lending, and in geographical locations relevant to TSB. In addition, we have 
maintained awareness of agriculture as a lending category and other sectors 
of the economy as employers of mortgage customers and relevant to business 
lending.
TSB has selected the NZBA sector level scenario analysis because it:
•	 Provides consistency in banking sector disclosure comparisons.
•	 Uses scenarios developed by the Network for Greening the Financial System 
(NGFS) as relevant to the banking sector.
•	 Has scenarios which meet Taskforce on Climate-related Financial 
Disclosures (TCFD) criteria of being plausible, distinctive, consistent, relevant 
and challenging.
•	 Bases scenarios on IPCC global reference scenarios and applying New 
Zealand climate parameters NIWA RCPs 2.6, 4.5 and 8.5 (lowest to highest 
emissions), and Climate Change Commission pathways, which provides 
additional plausibility and local relevance. 
13

Scenario analysis processes and governance 
For this disclosure, scenario analysis has been conducted as a standalone 
exercise with input across the bank. The project team that conducted 
the exercise reported to the Climate-related Disclosures project steering 
committee that includes a member of the executive leadership team (ELT) 
and members of the senior leadership team, and the Board has reviewed a 
summary of the scenarios and outputs. 
We engaged Mosaic to provide support for our scenario analysis processes 
(www.mosaicfsi.com/sustainability). No other external partners or stakeholders 
were involved in our entity level analysis, although contributions were also 
sought from industry peers and climate science and data providers , amongst 
others, as part of the sector level scenario analysis. 
TSB has not conducted our own modelling to produce the scenario narratives 
but utilised those provided in the NZBA analysis. TSB modelling, using physical 
risk data sourced from external providers (ClimSystems and Cotality), has 
been performed for assessment of scope and size of physical risks – see TSB 
Climate-related Risks and Opportunities below and the Risk Management 
section (page 24-26). 
In FY25 we conducted the first annual review of our scenarios and concluded 
that they continue to meet regulatory requirements and contribute to 
effectively assessing climate-related risks and opportunities and the resilience 
of TSB’s business model and strategy. We also held an initial discussion in 
FY25 with a key stakeholder for TSB, New Plymouth District Council, to gain an 
understanding of the climate scenarios that they are developing. Additionally, 
we expect to rerun scenario analysis when any sector level updates are issued 
or we become aware of material changes to drivers or outcomes in these 
narratives.
Our important work to integrate consideration of scenario analysis more 
fully into the strategy process has continued in FY25, and, as noted above, we 
have started the process to include external partners and stakeholders in our 
scenario analysis work.

TSB’s climate-related risk management processes have identified multiple risks based on the scenario analysis performed above. This disclosure reports on material

be prepared for any material risk.

assets and operations. The extent of the impacts is determined by the vulnerability of the exposed assets or operations.

financial consequences. The material risks disclosed below have been assessed as ‘High’ or above by the SRAM. Please 
refer to the Risk Management section for further details on our methodology.
We have elected to use adoption provision 2, so have not disclosed anticipated financial impacts for the material

Organisational level physical risks (any scenario)
TSB updated our previous physical risk assessment of our locations in FY25, including branches, offices, standalone 
ATMs, data centres and miscellaneous sites (e.g. carparks). To do this we used new data from physical climate models 
downscaled to New Zealand, and with high spatial resolution to assess organisational risk impacts at a more accurate 
level, and local data for sites initially identified as high or extreme risk. Of the properties reviewed, one branch was 
identified as a high risk due to the risk of river flooding and precipitation stress, but this was not rated as a material risk 
to TSB. The current immaturity of all climate models and limited availability of associated data means this assessment is 
indicative only.

TSB’s assessment of climate-related risks spans the short to long term. While all our Material Risk categories are given 
priority, TSB understands the importance of managing climate-related risks that extend beyond the typical time 
horizons for risk management. To support this, we apply an approach to climate-related risk materiality that considers 
risks associated with the plausible scenarios on an equal footing. This means climate-related risks that are assessed as 
‘High’ or above in any of the three climate scenarios are considered as material risks for the development of action plans

Our targets and ambition
Operational GHG emissions
TSB is committed to taking steps to contribute to the limiting of global warming and has set absolute GHG emissions reduction targets for Scope 1 and 2 GHG 
emissions that it considers ambitious but realistic. 
Our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions science-aligned target is a 42% reduction by FY30 from the FY23 emissions baseline. A science-aligned target meets SBTi (Science

choose to align with SBTi because they provide a clearly defined pathway to reduce GHG emissions, helping prevent the worst physical impacts of climate change and 
support business resilience. We have not submitted our target to SBTi for formal validation.
We have also set an ambition to reach net zero by 2050 for our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions.  This would be an absolute reduction, and is likely to require some use of 
offsets, as noted below. This ambition is aligned to SBTi guidance to contribute to limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

Emissions data for operational emissions is frequently based on estimates or proxy data and, as a result, provides an

droughts, heatwaves, extreme storms, or floods. 
Chronic: longer-term shifts in climate patterns are generally accepted to include rising sea 
levels, increased average temperatures and ocean acidification. These may lead to further 
development of chronic climate events, such as desertification. 
Transition
Policy and legal: Policy actions that attempt to constrain actions that contribute to the 
adverse effects of climate change or those that seek to promote adaptation to climate 
change. 
Technology: Improvements or innovations that support the transition to a lower-carbon, 
energy efficient economic system. Existing business models based on technologies likely to 
become superseded creates the need for adaptation to minimise the downside impact to 
remain competitive. 
Market: Shifts in supply and demand for certain commodities, products, and services as 
climate-related risks are considered. A change in human behaviour is required to transition to 
an economy with lower carbon emissions. The increased awareness of, and explicit demand 
for, climate-friendly financial products and investment are a potential trigger for businesses 
and banks to adjust their business strategies, notwithstanding potential regulatory or 
supervisory approaches.
Reputation: Changing customer or community perceptions of an organisation’s contribution 
to or detraction from the transition to a lower-carbon economy. Equity and debt investor 
awareness and expectations with respect to climate change are increasing.

Orderly transition 1.5°C
Overview
A future world where collective action is taken towards a low carbon global economy.
Description
In this scenario there is collective global climate action taken from the immediate term and the ambitious 
goals of the Paris Agreement are met, with governments worldwide moving forward simultaneously towards 
a low carbon economy. Regulations promoting low carbon products, services and operations, such as building 
energy efficiency standards, and additional industries subject to the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), are 
strengthened, and carbon prices rise steadily and significantly in the immediate and short term, adding costs 
to higher emitting industries including construction, transport and energy - all further promoting low-carbon 
producer and customer behaviour change. Consumers are well aware of the need to decarbonise the economy 
and therefore expect products and services, and residential and commercial properties, to be low emissions, 
and for businesses and other organisations to reduce their emissions in line with New Zealand and global 
carbon net zero by 2050. 
From the immediate term and continuing beyond the medium term, technology is steadily but rapidly 
developed to mitigate emissions such as electrification of transport and industry, carbon capture and 
sequestration and resilience (adaptation) measures. Fossil fuels are gradually phased out in favour of these 
low emissions technologies, and global electricity generation shifts towards fully renewable sources. In this 
scenario, the widespread policy support for low emissions technologies reduces reliance on afforestation to 
absorb residual emissions, allowing for greater rates of native afforestation. In the long term, policy support 
is provided for further mitigation actions and greater afforestation in order to maintain the net zero status 
including further emissions for remaining high-emitting sectors and greater use of emissions removals (Climate 
Change Commission, 2021).
As a result of this coordinated and timely action around the world to curb GHG emissions, emissions decline 
from the short term and reach net zero by 2040 in New Zealand (Ministry for the Environment, 2018. Climate 
Change Projections for New Zealand: Atmospheric Projections Based on Simulations from the IPCC Fifth 
Assessment, 2nd Edition) and 2050 globally, preventing the worst predicted physical impacts of climate change. 
However, the long-term chronic physical impacts from historic GHG emissions are still likely to occur, although 
to a less severe extent than the other scenarios.

Hothouse >3°C
Overview
Minimal action towards a low carbon global transition, increasing levels of social, economic, and environmental 
degradation.
Description
Hothouse is the ‘worst-case scenario’ of the three analysed, representing minimal action from the immediate to 
long term towards a low carbon global transition. There are minimal low carbon regulations and carbon pricing 
remains ineffectually low. As a result, there is little behaviour change and a lack of technology development and 
uptake. Fossil fuel use continues increasing as does mass consumption. 
Locally, New Zealand takes a slightly more proactive approach to climate action with existing policies such as 
retention of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) but with the global inertia there is limited public sentiment for 
substantial change. Action taken therefore is only enough to create a small reduction in domestic emissions. 
Adoption of low emissions technologies, already with only limited availability, largely only occurs where this 
is cost-saving rather than a change in societal expectations and behaviour. There continues to be high global 
demand for meat and dairy products up to the medium term, assisting New Zealand livestock farming. 
Renewable electricity share, already high in New Zealand, grows only very slightly, with global share growing 
but well under the more progressive scenarios. 
In this scenario, the retention of the New Zealand ETS and the high carbon price in the mid-2020s continues to 
generate a financial incentive to plant forests in the short term. In the medium term, the scale of forest planting 
scales back as the focus on meeting carbon budgets is lost but global growth in demand helps to provide 
incentives to expand forests around New Zealand for logging purposes, which sees exotic land area expand 
from 2.1Mha in the short term to 2.8Mha in the medium term (Climate Change Commission, 2021).
Despite increasing levels of social, economic and environmental degradation caused by the significantly 
worsening climate by the medium term, there is little shift in social and political traction towards a low 
emissions future.
The impact of these activities and inaction drives emissions higher throughout the remaining 21st century 
leading to significant materialisation of acute and chronic physical risks globally particularly from mid-century 
onwards. Heading into the medium term (the first half of the 21st century), this sees some increase in severity 
of extreme weather, later accompanied by rising sea levels beyond the medium term resulting in high physical 
risk. This threatens coastal developments worldwide, placing pressure on global relations. Overall, when 
considered alongside the Orderly Transition and Too Little Too Late scenarios, this scenario represents low 
transition impacts and a high level of physical impacts.

•	 The methodology shown above represents a modification to the standard PCAF approach for this lending (agriculture

We have used the alternative methodology in the table above, based on land area and use, due to the limited

Description of procedures performed
Procedures performed in a limited assurance engagement vary in nature and timing from, and are less in extent than, for 
a reasonable assurance engagement. Consequently, the level of assurance obtained in a limited assurance engagement 
is substantially lower than the assurance that would have been obtained had a reasonable assurance engagement been 
performed. Our procedures were designed to obtain a limited level of assurance on which to base our conclusion and do 
not provide all the evidence that would be required to provide a reasonable level of assurance.
Our procedures did not include testing controls or performing procedures relating to checking aggregation or calculation 
of data within IT systems.
A limited assurance engagement consists of making enquiries, primarily of persons responsible for preparing the report 
and related information and applying analytical and other relevant procedures. 
Our procedures included:
•	
Obtaining, through inquiries, an understanding of TSB’s control environment, processes and information systems 
relevant to the preparation of the GHG Disclosures. We did not evaluate the design of particular control activities, or 
obtain evidence about their implementation;
•	
Evaluating whether TSB’s methods for developing estimates are appropriate and had been consistently applied. 
Our procedures did not include testing the data on which the estimates are based or separately developing our own 
estimates against which to evaluate TSB’s estimates;
•	
Testing a limited number of items to, or from, supporting records, as appropriate;
•	
Performing analytical procedures on particular emission categories by comparing the expected GHGs emitted to 
reported GHGs emitted and made inquiries of management to obtain explanations for any significant differences we 
identified and where necessary, perform additional tests of detail; and
•	
Considering the presentation and disclosure of the GHG disclosures.
